The problem currently looks like a runtime scheduling or symbol-selection defect between the visible tape model, the due-symbol planning logic, and the one-by-one progressive quote request loop.

Audit the full path from tape composition through quote scheduling and scene application, including StartupCoordinator, tape view-model generation, due-symbol selection, and the code that chooses the next symbol(s) for YFinance.NET requests.

Instrument the runtime more deeply if needed so each tape lane reports: visible symbols, symbols considered due, symbols actually requested, symbols returned, and symbols finally applied to the rendered lane.
Verify whether duplicate symbols across tapes, ancillary symbol deduplication, or lane ordering are starving some tape symbols indefinitely under the current 500 ms progressive cadence.
Verify whether some tape groups are present in the rendered scene but absent from the refresh candidate pool after recent YFinance-only and single-source cleanup work.

current_priority_backlog.title: Extract a clean service-ready data engine boundary between retrieval/orchestration and UI rendering
evidence: User requested a major refactor to cleanly separate data retrieval from UI rendering so the architecture can later support a Windows service and more controlled provider parallelism.
notes: Superseded in Beta 5.6 by NB-031, which replaces the earlier in-process DataEngine / optional Windows service direction with a cleaner client-server architecture centered on an external YFinance.NET server process and a thinner UI client.

Manual code-review validation summary: the core diagnosis remains correct, but the ticket must explicitly account for three seams that are easy to underestimate. First, StartupCoordinator is not just long; it directly constructs concrete infrastructure such as multiple provider implementations, ProviderHealthService, FinanceNewsService, ScreensaverSettingsService, SymbolProfileStore, and ExchangePhotoCacheService. At the time of that review it also still constructed QuoteCacheService, but that app-level quote cache has since been removed. Second, settings, secrets, traces, and caches are still user-profile rooted through PathHelper and ProviderSecretStoreService, which means a future service-ready engine needs explicit settings/secrets abstractions rather than assuming those concerns can stay ambient. Third, several orchestration types still live under the PortfolioSaver.Screensaver.Services namespace even though the product is desktop-first, so namespace and composition cleanup should be treated as part of the refactor rather than deferred as mere polish.

Current diagnosis: the repository already has a meaningful provider layer under src/PortfolioSaver.Data and domain models under src/PortfolioSaver.Core, but the main runtime orchestration still lives in src/PortfolioSaver.Presentation/Services/StartupCoordinator.cs. StartupCoordinator is approximately 1800 lines and currently owns quote scheduling, provider fallback ordering, startup warmup policy, graph warmup, news refresh orchestration, cache usage, freshness logic, tracing, and scene-shaping decisions. ScreensaverSceneControl is over 2100 lines and still depends on some of that orchestration behavior directly. FinanceNewsService and ScreensaverSettingsService also sit in the same runtime namespace, reinforcing that the retrieval/runtime layer is not yet cleanly separated from the product surface.

The goal of this ticket is not merely to prepare for a future Windows service. The deeper goal is to establish a stable architectural seam that improves concurrency, testability, startup behavior, scheduling clarity, and future maintainability while keeping the existing desktop product working throughout the migration.

Target architecture: keep PortfolioSaver.Core for immutable models, enums, validation rules, and provider policy definitions; keep PortfolioSaver.Data for raw provider clients, caches, symbol metadata, and persistence helpers; introduce a new middle layer such as PortfolioSaver.DataEngine for quote scheduling, provider execution planning, budget/rate-limit enforcement, snapshot aggregation, startup/warmup policy, historical warmup coordination, and news scheduling; leave PortfolioSaver.Presentation focused on view-model shaping, animation, scene-state rendering, and UX display policy. Introduce explicit abstractions for settings access, secret resolution, cache paths, trace sinks, and clock/network probes so the engine is not tied directly to user-profile helpers or UI-era service classes. A future PortfolioSaver.DataService host may run the same DataEngine later, but the refactor should not depend on introducing a Windows service immediately.

Non-goal: do not attempt a big-bang rewrite, do not re-architect the locked VM harness in the process, and do not start by adding arbitrary multithreading. Parallel provider execution should be a controlled outcome of the new engine boundary, not the first step.

Phase 0 - dependency audit and boundary contracts: before moving logic, catalog every concrete dependency currently new'ed inside StartupCoordinator and related runtime services, then introduce abstractions for settings access, secret resolution, cache/storage access, trace logging, network availability, time, and provider factories. Acceptance: DataEngine can be composed from contracts rather than constructing environment-bound helpers internally.

Phase 1 - seam definition: define engine-facing contracts for quote snapshots, quote-refresh requests/results, provider execution plans, freshness anchors, startup readiness, and historical/news work items. During this phase, copy as little behavior as possible; prefer extracting interfaces and pure helper types first. Acceptance: Presentation can depend on an engine contract instead of directly owning provider ladder decisions.

Phase 2 - extract scheduler and provider orchestration: move refresh-window building, due-symbol selection, stagger logic, provider plan ordering, rate-limit cooldown handling, partial-result handling, and quote-merge logic out of StartupCoordinator into DataEngine services. Keep concurrency behavior semantically equivalent at first. Acceptance: unit tests can validate scheduling and provider fallback behavior without constructing WPF controls or scene state.

Phase 3 - extract startup/warmup and freshness policies: move initial stale-data recovery logic, dedicated Yahoo warmup rules, graph warmup coordination, startup readiness thresholds, and status freshness anchor calculation into the engine layer. Acceptance: the engine can produce a clean startup state model such as loading, warming, live, partial, stale without the scene control owning the logic directly.

Phase 4 - extract news orchestration and runtime settings access: move summarized news scheduling, feed selection cadence, cache decisions, and teleprinter item preparation into engine-facing services while keeping the visual teleprinter playback itself in Presentation. At the same time, split settings read/write concerns from runtime settings consumption so the engine depends on a read model rather than the settings UI service classes directly. Acceptance: news retrieval and news rendering become distinct responsibilities and the engine is no longer coupled to ScreensaverSettingsService.

Phase 5 - scene adaptation and namespace cleanup: reduce StartupCoordinator to a thin adapter that asks DataEngine for a state snapshot and maps that into ScreensaverSceneState and view models. Rename or relocate residual runtime classes out of PortfolioSaver.Screensaver.Services where appropriate so the desktop-first architecture is reflected clearly. Acceptance: StartupCoordinator becomes a compositional facade instead of the core runtime brain, and service names/namespaces no longer imply legacy ownership of the modern runtime layer.

Phase 6 - optional controlled concurrency: once the engine owns scheduling, add bounded async worker lanes by concern or provider group, for example Yahoo quotes, provider fallbacks, historical warmup, news, and treasury/macros. Use bounded concurrency, explicit cooldown/budget gates, deterministic merge rules, and structured tracing. Acceptance: parallelism improves cadence without introducing nondeterministic UI regressions.

Phase 7 - future service host feasibility review: only after the in-process DataEngine is stable should we evaluate adding a PortfolioSaver.DataService Windows service host. That later review must explicitly address secrets ownership, per-user versus machine-wide settings, IPC contract choice such as named pipes or gRPC over named pipes, installer behavior, and support burden. This ticket does not require implementing the service host itself.

Key risks to manage: duplicated logic during migration, freshness regressions, cache/secrets path confusion, over-eager concurrency creating race conditions, over-coupling the engine to user-profile storage, and accidental coupling back from Presentation into the engine. Mitigations: move one concern at a time, keep trace semantics stable, add regression tests before each extraction, and insist on small commits that preserve the canonical VM proof path.

Required regression coverage during the refactor: scheduling tests, provider fallback tests, stale/fresh classification tests, startup readiness tests, news cadence tests, graph warmup tests, settings/secrets abstraction tests, and at each major phase a canonical VM proof through the locked harness. No phase should be considered complete if local tests are green but the canonical VM path is broken.

Definition of done for the full ticket: a new engine layer exists; StartupCoordinator is dramatically reduced and no longer owns most provider orchestration logic; Presentation consumes engine snapshots rather than managing retrieval policy directly; provider scheduling is testable without WPF; settings and secret access are abstracted cleanly enough that a later service host would not require another deep untangling; the canonical VM harness remains the validation baseline; and the resulting architecture is ready for a later optional Windows service host without forcing another major refactor.
Deferred from the current beta lane to the next major release so the refactor can be planned and executed as a deliberate architecture program rather than mixed into current stabilization work.
Not a beta-blocker for the current lane as long as the existing locked harness and data/UI behavior remain stable enough for ongoing product fixes.

current_priority_backlog.title: Replace the in-process YFinance runtime with a standalone YFinance.NET client-server architecture
evidence: User requested replacing the old service-ready DataEngine concept with a pure client-server architecture where YFinance.NET runs as its own process and the UI becomes a sequential client.
notes: This ticket completely replaces NB-023 as the active architecture program.
Separate YFinance.NET fully into its own process with its own circular log file and runtime lifecycle.
The YFinance.NET server must listen on TCP port 14870 and accept client connections from any IP address.
The server must support multiple client connections with a maximum of 1024 concurrent clients.
Design the server so it can run on a completely separate machine from the UI client in the future.

Long-range portability target: keep the architecture and protocol clean enough that the YFinance.NET server can later be reimplemented or migrated to cross-platform standard C++ for Linux/Unix/Windows/Windows-XP/macOS Intel/macOS ARM/Raspberry Pi and related platforms.
Define a network protocol between the UI and the YFinance.NET server, ideally echoing the clarity of Yahoo v7-style request/response semantics, while remaining our own stable product protocol.

Document the protocol in a dedicated Interface Control Document (ICD) kept in the project repository, and treat that ICD as a maintained project artifact that evolves with implementation changes and test expectations.

The client-server protocol must be minimal but sufficient: no speculative complexity, but enough structure to cleanly support the required request types, cache semantics, server metadata, and explicit error states.

Protocol responses must include explicit exception scenarios the UI can handle cleanly, such as Network Lost, Upstream Server Not Responding, upstream throttled, invalid symbol, and cache miss or stale-result states where relevant.

Async server messages are limited to server or connection lifecycle events, not ordinary market-data flow. Normal quote/history/timing failures should be returned as request-scoped error responses, not unsolicited pushes.
Primary protocol model: client-driven request/response. The UI client owns request initiation and pacing; the server answers requests and does not become the UI scheduler.

Ordinary lookup and upstream failures must remain request-scoped error responses. Async server exception messages are reserved for server-wide or connection-wide conditions such as shutdown, overload, idle timeout, or protocol violation.

Preserve upstream-sync friendliness: the clean-room YFinance.NET port must remain easy to keep in sync with future changes from the user's upstream Python fork, and the new client-server split must not destroy that maintainability goal.

YFinance.NET server behavior for single or batch ticker requests: first check cache, return cached values when they are newer than the 10-minute freshness ceiling, otherwise fetch from Yahoo, return the fresh data, and store it back in cache.
Nothing served from cache should be older than 10 minutes unless the protocol intentionally marks it as stale under a future degraded-mode extension.

Any client identifier sent upstream to Yahoo must be a unique random hash derived from the requesting machine identity and must not include the author name, organization name, or other human-identifying product branding.

Once the caching YFinance.NET server is functional, the UI should no longer carry throttling responsibility. The UI should request macros one by one during warmup, then global exchanges one by one, then continue sequential retrieval from YFinance.NET with approximately 500 milliseconds (0.5 seconds) spacing after each UI update so visual update flares remain continuous while CPU load stays controlled.

No parallel connections from the same UI client to YFinance.NET. Multi-client server support exists so one shared server can eventually support many desktop UIs across a network, not so a single UI floods the server with parallel requests.

Server lifecycle must support two modes: owned mode and standalone mode. The default product mode for now is owned mode, where the UI launches the YFinance.NET server and the server exits when the owning UI process or session goes away.

UI configuration changes should normally affect only client-side request sequencing and symbol selection. They should not generally mutate server internals; the server should expose only a small admin/control surface such as health, status, optional shutdown, and optional cache flush operations.

This is a major refactor and includes test script updates, harness updates, starting and stopping YFinance.NET alongside the UI for now, documentation updates, and forensic code-review cleanup revealed during the transition.

Acceptance should include a clean end-to-end UI proof with the standalone YFinance.NET server process, updated harness lifecycle management, updated docs, and removal of obsolete in-process retrieval assumptions from the active code path.
Protocol and implementation design are now captured in docs/YFINANCE_NET_ICD.md and docs/YFINANCE_NET_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md as the starting baseline for execution.
Implemented YFinance.NET.Protocol, YFinance.NET.Client, and YFinance.NET.Server as the active client-server runtime boundary.
The standalone server now listens on TCP 14870, binds to any IP, supports owned and standalone modes, and advertises a maximum of 1024 concurrent clients.
All request, response, and async event messages now carry a local-time timestamp with UTC offset plus an uppercase SHA-256 payload checksum.

All client/server communications are now logged into the dedicated UI and YFinance circular trace files, including request send/receive, response send/receive, integrity verification, and lifecycle events.
PortfolioSaver quote, history, market-timing, ticker-info, and config-validation paths now go through the TCP client seam rather than calling YFinance in-process.
